name: Gangtok and East Sikkim
tagline: Monasteries, high lakes and the old Silk Route
meta_description: Plan Gangtok and East Sikkim on a fair budget: Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La, Zuluk's Silk Route, Rumtek, permits, shared jeeps, month-by-month advice and real costs.
summary: East Sikkim is Gangtok plus everything within a day of it: Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La at 3,700–4,300 m, the old wool road through Zuluk, and the monasteries of Rumtek and Ranka. Go October to May, sleep in Gangtok, and budget for permits and Gangtok-registered vehicles.
intro: Gangtok sits on a ridge at about 1,650 m, and almost everything in East Sikkim is measured from it. Two hours up the Nathu La road you reach Tsomgo Lake at 3,753 m, then the border pass itself at 4,310 m. An hour across the valley is Rumtek, seat in exile of the Karmapa. Four hours east, past the old bazaar at Rongli, the road climbs to Zuluk and the zigzags that once carried mule trains towards Tibet.

Since the 2021 reorganisation, the old East Sikkim district is split in two. Gangtok district covers the capital, Tsomgo, Nathu La, Rumtek, Ranka and the Fambong Lho forests. The new Pakyong district holds the airport at Pakyong, Rongli, Rhenock, Aritar and the Silk Route villages of Zuluk and Nathang. We keep calling the whole area East Sikkim, as most drivers and hotels still do.

This is the busiest corner of Sikkim, and it is easy to overspend. Hotel rates double in the Puja weeks of October and in May–June, and almost every high-altitude trip runs in a Gangtok-registered vehicle with a permit. The way to save is simple: travel in March, November or early December, share vehicles, sleep central so you can walk, and eat where Gangtok's office workers eat.

The stories here are worth the trip on their own. Gangtok was a small monastery hamlet until the Chogyal moved his court here in 1894. Sikkim was a separate kingdom until 1975. The Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali-speaking Gorkha communities each have their own festivals, food and histories. We point you to the places where those stories are still visible, not just the viewpoints.

story.title: From a Himalayan kingdom to India's 22nd state
paras: Sikkim's royal line began in 1642, when Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated as the first Chogyal, or dharma king, at Yuksom in the west. The capital moved from Yuksom to Rabdentse and then Tumlong. In 1861 the Treaty of Tumlong made Sikkim a British protectorate in all but name, and in 1894 the ninth Chogyal, Thutob Namgyal, shifted the court to Gangtok. A small settlement of monks and farmers became the capital.

Gangtok grew as the gateway to Tibet. Wool, musk and salt came down over Nathu La and Jelep La; cloth, sugar and tea went up. The royal chapel at Tsuklakhang hosted coronations and weddings. Under a 1950 treaty, Sikkim became an Indian protectorate while keeping its king. Palden Thondup Namgyal, the last Chogyal, was crowned in 1965, two years after marrying the American Hope Cooke.

The 1970s brought political unrest and pressure for democratic reform. In a referendum on 14 April 1975, voters backed abolishing the monarchy, and on 16 May 1975 Sikkim became India's 22nd state, with Kazi Lhendup Dorjee as first Chief Minister. People in Sikkim still hold different views about how the merger came about. What everyone agrees on is that the palace chapel, the dances and the old families of Gangtok keep that royal past in daily view.

did_you_know: Gangtok has been Sikkim's capital only since 1894, when Thutob Namgyal moved the royal court there from Tumlong.
Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016.
The 14th Dalai Lama laid the foundation stone of the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology in Gangtok in 1957, and Jawaharlal Nehru opened it in 1958.
Nathu La was sealed after the 1962 war and reopened for India–China border trade only in 2006.
Aritar's Dak Bungalow was built in 1895 by John Claude White, the first British Political Officer in Sikkim.

highlights.title: Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La in one day
highlights.text: Leave Gangtok at 7 am and climb 2,600 m in under three hours to a glacial lake at 3,753 m and the India–China border at 4,310 m. Baba Harbhajan Singh's shrine sits on the way. Indian nationals only for Nathu La, Wednesday to Sunday.

highlights.title: Zuluk and the Silk Route zigzags
highlights.text: The old Kalimpong–Lhasa mule road climbs from Rongli through Zuluk to Nathang and Kupup. Sleep in a village homestay at 2,900 m, watch sunrise over Kangchenjunga from Thambi viewpoint, then drive the loops that photographers come for. Permit needed; not open to foreigners.

highlights.title: Gangtok's royal and monastic core
highlights.text: Walk from MG Marg to Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel, then on to the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology and Do Drul Chorten. Most of it costs under ₹100 and fits in one unhurried day, with momos on MG Marg at the end.

highlights.title: Rumtek, seat of the Karmapa in exile
highlights.text: The 16th Karmapa rebuilt Rumtek after fleeing Tibet in 1959 and opened it on Losar 1966. Visit the main hall, the golden stupa with his relics and Old Rumtek lower down, then loop back via Lingdum Monastery at Ranka.

highlights.title: Aritar and Lampokhari Lake
highlights.text: A quiet village at about 1,400 m with one of Sikkim's oldest natural lakes, a British dak bungalow from 1895 and forest walks. It is the easy first night on the Silk Route and far cheaper than Gangtok.

highlights.title: Winter festivals in Gangtok
highlights.text: Early December brings the Kagyed masked dances at Tsuklakhang and then Losoong, the Bhutia harvest new year. Days are clear and cold, the Kangchenjunga range is sharp, and hotel rates drop after the October rush.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then drive about 115–125 km up NH10 along the Teesta to Gangtok, normally 4–5 hours. Shared jeeps from Siliguri and NJP cost about ₹400–600 a seat and SNT buses ₹275–500, indicative 2026. A reserved small car costs ₹4,000–5,500, an Innova ₹5,500–7,500. Pakyong Airport, 31 km south of Gangtok, has no scheduled commercial flights as of 2026, and the Sevoke–Rangpo railway is still under construction, targeted for about 2027. In the monsoon, NH10 is often cut by landslides; drivers then detour via Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock or via Lava and Rorathang, adding 2–3 hours. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian nationals need no permit to enter Sikkim but need a Protected Area Permit, arranged by a registered Gangtok agent with photos and ID, for Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir, Nathu La and the Silk Route beyond Rongli. Nathu La is open to Indians only, Wednesday to Sunday. Foreign nationals need a free Restricted Area Permit (Inner Line Permit) to enter Sikkim, available online and at Rangpo; they can visit Tsomgo on a day permit in a group, but not Nathu La or Zuluk. Sikkim also charges a ₹50 tourist fee at hotel check-in. Check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: East Sikkim gets expensive in three places: peak-week hotel rates, reserved Gangtok vehicles for the passes, and resort food. Cut the first by travelling in March, November or early December. Cut the second by buying shared seats for Tsomgo and Nathu La and sharing a Silk Route car with another couple. Cut the third by sleeping near MG Marg and eating momos, thukpa and thalis where locals eat.
costs: Village homestay, Zuluk or Aritar, with meals
tips: Book the Nathu La permit for a Wednesday or Thursday, when quotas are less contested than at weekends.
Use Gangtok's local shared taxis at ₹20–40 a seat instead of hiring a car for every hop around town.
Ask your Silk Route homestay for full board; it costs less than eating out and there are few restaurants anyway.
Skip the paid coat and boot hire at Tsomgo in October and May if you have a warm jacket and closed shoes.
Avoid the Durga Puja and Diwali weeks if you can: the same room often costs 50–100% more than in November.

months.weather: Gangtok 4–13 °C, dry, cold nights; snow at Tsomgo
months.summary: January is cold and mostly clear. Gangtok mornings are crisp with good mountain views, and Tsomgo Lake is usually frozen. The catch is snow on the high roads: Nathu La and the Kupup–Nathang stretch can close for days. Lower places such as Rumtek and Aritar are pleasant and quiet. It is a good month for travellers who want low rates and do not mind cancelling a pass day.
months.tip: Book Tsomgo and Nathu La for the middle of your stay so a snow closure does not wipe out the trip.
months.price_note: After New Year week, Gangtok hotel rates drop sharply and many offer 20–40% off rack rates.

months.weather: Gangtok 5–15 °C, mostly dry, frost higher up
months.summary: February warms slowly. Losar, the Tibetan new year, often falls this month, bringing prayers at Rumtek and family celebrations in Gangtok. Tsomgo is still frozen or half frozen, which many visitors want to see, but snow can block the road beyond. Views of Kangchenjunga stay good on most mornings. Crowds are thin and rates are low.
months.tip: Carry proper winter layers for Tsomgo: at 3,753 m it is often below freezing even at noon.
months.price_note: Low season for hotels; good deals on comfort-tier rooms, except over Losar holiday weekends.

months.summary: March is one of our favourite months. The high roads usually reopen, rhododendrons start to flower at lower altitudes, and Gangtok is mild. Tsomgo may still have ice at the edges. The Silk Route is quiet and homestays have rooms. Haze can soften the mountain views later in the month, so go for the early mornings.
months.tip: Book Zuluk for late March or April if you want rhododendrons along the climb from Padamchen.
months.price_note: Shoulder-season rates; Silk Route vehicle packages are easier to bargain before Holi and Easter weekends.

months.summary: April is rhododendron season around Kyongnosla, Zuluk and Fambong Lho, and the high lakes thaw. Days are warm in Gangtok with occasional afternoon showers. Nathu La and the Silk Route are open most days. Crowds start building towards the end of the month as school holidays approach in some states.
months.tip: Start pass days early; afternoon cloud and showers become common from mid-April.
months.price_note: Rates rise in the second half of April as the summer season begins.

months.summary: May is peak season. Tsomgo is open water, Nathu La and Nathang are clear of snow on most days, and families from across India fill Gangtok. It is pleasant but busy and pricier. Saga Dawa, the holiest Buddhist month, sometimes starts late in May, with prayers and a procession in Gangtok.
months.tip: Book Nathu La permits two days ahead; quotas fill in May.
months.price_note: Peak rates; book hotels and vehicles early, and expect 30–60% above winter prices.

months.summary: Early June still works, especially for Gangtok and the monasteries, but the monsoon usually arrives by the middle of the month. Landslides begin on NH10 and the Silk Route. Saga Dawa often falls in June, a good time to be in Gangtok. Keep plans flexible and lower your hopes for mountain views.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before your flight out of Bagdogra in case NH10 closes.
months.price_note: Rates stay high in the first half of June with school holidays, then fall as the rain sets in.

months.summary: July is the wettest stretch. NH10 is frequently cut by landslides, the Silk Route and high roads close often, and views are rare. If you do come, stay in Gangtok, see the monasteries and the town, and travel with a flexible return. It is quiet, green and very cheap, but not the trip most people imagine.
months.tip: Check NH10 status every evening before a travel day and avoid driving after dark in rain.
months.price_note: Lowest rates of the year; many hotels discount 40–50% but some smaller ones close.

months.summary: August is still monsoon. Landslides on NH10 and in North Sikkim make road travel unpredictable. Late in the month, Pang Lhabsol may bring the warrior dances to Tsuklakhang. Monasteries and Gangtok's town walks remain the safe options. We do not recommend Zuluk or Nathang this month.
months.tip: Carry leech socks and a light rain jacket if you plan any forest walks.
months.price_note: Deep off-season rates; book flexible, refundable rooms.

months.summary: September is a transition month. The rain eases through the second half, the hills are green and the first clear mornings return. Pang Lhabsol is often celebrated at Tsuklakhang this month. Roads can still be patchy, so keep a buffer. Late September is a good value window before the October rush.
months.tip: Book October trips by early September; Puja-week rooms and vehicles sell out.
months.price_note: Rates are low until the last week, then jump ahead of Durga Puja.

months.summary: October brings clear skies, dry roads and the best mountain views of the year, and with them the biggest crowds. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays fill Gangtok with families from Kolkata and beyond. Everything is open: Tsomgo, Nathu La, Zuluk, Nathang and Kupup. Book early and avoid the main holiday weeks if you can.
months.tip: If you must travel in Puja week, book shared seats for passes two days ahead and eat early to avoid queues.
months.price_note: Peak rates in Puja and Diwali weeks, often 50–100% above November.

months.summary: November is the sweet spot. The sky is clear, the crowds have gone home, and rates fall. The Silk Route is at its best: Thambi viewpoint sunrises, clear views from Nathang and Kupup, and frost on the yak pastures. Nights get cold above 2,500 m, so bring proper layers.
months.tip: Pack thermals and a down jacket for Zuluk and Nathang, where nights drop below freezing.
months.price_note: Good-value month; after the first week many hotels discount 20–30%.

months.summary: December is clear and cold, with crisp mountain views most mornings. The Kagyed dances at Tsuklakhang and Losoong, the Bhutia harvest new year, bring Gangtok's festival season. Snow can close Nathu La and the high Silk Route road for days, so keep backups. Rates are good until the Christmas and New Year week.
months.tip: Pair the Kagyed dance and Losoong in one trip in the first half of December.
months.price_note: Low rates in early December; prices spike from about 23 December to New Year.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Gangtok and East Sikkim
faqs.a: October to mid-December and March to May are best. October and November give the clearest views; March and April bring rhododendrons; May is warm but crowded. Avoid July and August, when landslides often block NH10 and the high roads. December to February is cold but clear, with snow that can close Nathu La for days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Gangtok and East Sikkim
faqs.a: Plan at least 4 nights: one day for Gangtok's monasteries and MG Marg, one for Tsomgo and Nathu La, one for Rumtek and Ranka, and a buffer for weather. Add 2–3 nights for the Silk Route through Aritar and Zuluk. With 7 nights you can do all of it without rushing or doubling back on long drives.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Gangtok
faqs.a: No permit is needed to enter Sikkim or to stay in Gangtok. Indian nationals need a Protected Area Permit only for restricted areas such as Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir, Nathu La and the Silk Route beyond Rongli. Registered Gangtok agents arrange it with two photos and a photo ID copy. Sikkim also charges a ₹50 tourist fee at hotel check-in; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La and Zuluk
faqs.a: Foreigners can visit Tsomgo Lake on a day permit arranged by a registered agent, usually in a group of two or more, after getting the free Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Nathu La and the Silk Route through Zuluk, Nathang and Kupup are closed to foreign nationals. Rules change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get from Bagdogra airport to Gangtok
faqs.a: Take a reserved car from the Bagdogra prepaid counter for about ₹4,000–5,500 in a small car or ₹5,500–7,500 in an Innova, indicative 2026. The 125 km drive takes 4.5–5.5 hours. On a budget, take a local cab to Siliguri and a shared jeep for ₹400–600 a seat. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights as of 2026.

faqs.q: How much does a budget trip to Gangtok cost per day
faqs.a: A careful traveller can manage about ₹2,500–3,500 per person per day, indicative 2026, sharing a budget room near MG Marg, eating local food and using shared taxis. Pass days cost more: a shared seat for Tsomgo and Nathu La runs ₹1,500–2,500. A 5-night Gangtok and Darjeeling package starts around ₹14,000–16,000 per person.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to Gangtok in the monsoon
faqs.a: Gangtok itself is safe, but the roads are the problem. From mid-June to September, landslides often close NH10 for hours or days, and high routes such as Nathu La, Zuluk and North Sikkim may shut. If you go, keep spare days, avoid driving after dark in rain, book refundable rooms and check current status before you travel.

Tsomgo Lake is usually frozen or partly frozen from about late December to March, and sometimes into April in a cold year. January and February are the surest months. Snow can also close the road at this time, so keep a buffer day. From May to November the lake is open water, with autumn bringing the clearest skies.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness at Nathu La
faqs.a: Some people feel headaches, breathlessness or nausea at Tsomgo and Nathu La, which sit at 3,753 m and 4,310 m. Sleep at least one night in Gangtok first, drink water, avoid alcohol the night before, walk slowly and limit time at the top to 30–45 minutes. Anyone with heart or lung problems should ask a doctor before going.
